title: Pinyin, Tones & Chinese Characters
description: The building blocks of Mandarin: pinyin spelling, initials and finals, the four tones and neutral tone, and how characters are built from strokes and radicals.

notes.heading: 📌 What is Pinyin?
notes.body:
Pinyin (拼音 pīnyīn, literally 'spell sounds') is the official system for writing Mandarin Chinese sounds using the Roman alphabet. It was developed in the 1950s and is now used worldwide to teach pronunciation, type Chinese on keyboards, and look up words in dictionaries.

Every Chinese character has exactly one syllable, and pinyin spells out that syllable:

| Character | Pinyin | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 妈 | mā | mum |
| 你 | nǐ | you |
| 好 | hǎo | good |
| 中 | zhōng | middle / China |

🔑 **How it works:** pinyin is a *tool*, not a replacement for characters. Chinese people write with characters; pinyin just tells you how to say them. Learn pinyin well at the start and every new word you meet becomes easier to pronounce.

notes.heading: 🔑 Initials and Finals
notes.body:
Almost every Mandarin syllable is made of two parts:

- **Initial (声母 shēngmǔ)** — the starting consonant
- **Final (韵母 yùnmǔ)** — the vowel part that follows

Common initials:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| b | p | m | f |
| d | t | n | l |
| g | k | h | |
| j | q | x | |
| zh | ch | sh | r |
| z | c | s | |

Common finals: **a, o, e, i, u, ü** and compound finals such as **ai, ei, ao, ou, an, en, ang, eng**.

💡 **Worked Example:**
- mā = initial **m** + final **a**
- hǎo = initial **h** + final **ao**
- zhōng = initial **zh** + final **ong**

📎 **Key Points:**
- Some syllables have no initial at all: ā (啊), ài (爱, love).
- After **j, q, x**, the final ü is written as a plain u: jū, qù, xuě — but still pronounced ü.

notes.heading: 🎵 The Four Tones and the Neutral Tone
notes.body:
Mandarin is a **tonal language**: the pitch pattern of a syllable is part of the word. The same letters with different tones are completely different words.

| Tone | Name | Sound | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| First tone | high-level | high and flat, like singing a note | 妈 mā — mum |
| Second tone | rising | rises, like asking 'yes?' in English | 麻 má — hemp |
| Third tone | falling-rising | dips down then up | 马 mǎ — horse |
| Fourth tone | falling | falls sharply, like a command | 骂 mà — to scold |
| Neutral tone | light | short and light, no tone mark | 吗 ma — question particle |

💡 **Worked Example:** mā, má, mǎ, mà, ma — five different words from the same letters!

⚠️ **Common Mistake:** when two third tones meet, the first one changes to a second tone in natural speech. 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but pronounced **ní hǎo**. This is called third-tone sandhi.

notes.heading: ✍️ Where Does the Tone Mark Go?
notes.body:
The tone mark sits on top of **one vowel** in the final. Follow these rules in order:

1. If the syllable contains **a** or **o**, the mark goes there: m**ā**, h**à**o, h**ō**ng.
2. Otherwise, if it contains **e**, the mark goes on e: h**ē**, m**è**i.
3. For the pairs **iu** and **ui**, the mark goes on the *second* vowel: li**ù** (six), shu**ǐ** (water).
4. When the mark sits on **i**, the dot of the i disappears: n**ǐ**, m**í**.

💡 **Worked Example:**
- xiǎo (small) — a is present, so the mark sits on a.
- duì (correct) — a ui pair, so the mark sits on the second vowel, i.
- shuǐ (water) — same ui rule, mark on i.

📎 **Key Points:**
- Only one tone mark per syllable, always on a vowel, never on a consonant.
- The **neutral tone has no mark at all**: 妈妈 māma, 谢谢 xièxie, 我们 wǒmen.

notes.heading: 🖊️ Strokes and Stroke Order
notes.body:
Chinese characters are written with basic strokes (笔画 bǐhuà). The most common ones:

| Stroke | Name | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| 一 | héng | horizontal, left → right |
| 丨 | shù | vertical, top → bottom |
| 丿 | piě | left-falling sweep |
| ㇏ | nà | right-falling sweep |
| 丶 | diǎn | dot |

🔑 **Stroke order rules (笔顺 bǐshùn):**
1. **Top before bottom**: 三 (three) — write the top line first.
2. **Left before right**: 明 (bright) — write 日 before 月.
3. **Horizontal before vertical**: 十 (ten) — the horizontal line crosses first.
4. **Outside before inside, close last**: 国 (country) — frame, then the inside, then the bottom line seals it.
5. **Centre before the two sides**: 小 (small) — the middle vertical hook, then the two dots.

📎 **Why it matters:** correct stroke order makes your characters balanced, faster to write, and readable to others — and it helps you count strokes when using a dictionary.

notes.heading: 🔍 Radicals: Meaning Clues Inside Characters
notes.body:
A **radical (部首 bùshǒu)** is a component of a character that usually hints at its meaning. Learning common radicals lets you guess what unfamiliar characters are about.

| Radical | Meaning | Example characters |
|---|---|---|
| 氵 (water) | water, liquids | 河 hé river · 海 hǎi sea |
| 口 (mouth) | mouth, eating, speaking | 吃 chī eat · 喝 hē drink |
| 女 (woman) | female | 妈 mā mum · 姐 jiě older sister |
| 木 (tree) | wood, trees | 树 shù tree · 林 lín woods |
| 亻 (person) | people | 你 nǐ you · 他 tā he |
| 讠 (speech) | speaking, words | 说 shuō speak · 话 huà speech |

💡 **Worked Example:** you meet the character 湖. You don't know it, but the 氵 radical tells you it has something to do with water — in fact 湖 hú means 'lake'.

📎 **Key Point:** dictionaries organise characters by radical, so knowing radicals also helps you look words up.

notes.heading: 🧱 Simple Characters, Compound Characters & Why Tones Matter
notes.body:
**Simple characters (独体字 dútǐzì)** cannot be split into smaller meaningful parts. Many began as pictures:

- 人 rén — person (two legs walking)
- 口 kǒu — mouth
- 日 rì — sun
- 月 yuè — moon
- 木 mù — tree

**Compound characters (合体字 hétǐzì)** combine two or more parts:

- 明 míng (bright) = 日 sun + 月 moon — the two brightest things in the sky
- 林 lín (woods) = 木 + 木 — two trees
- 好 hǎo (good) = 女 woman + 子 child

Many compound characters pair a **meaning part (radical)** with a **sound part**: 妈 mā = 女 (female meaning) + 马 mǎ (sound clue).

⚠️ **Why tones matter:** a wrong tone gives a wrong word, sometimes with embarrassing results:
- 买 mǎi (to buy) vs 卖 mài (to sell) — opposite meanings!
- 问 wèn (to ask) vs 吻 wěn (to kiss)

✅ **Check:** if you can explain why 明 means bright and name the radical in 河, you are ready to learn characters much faster.

flashcards.definition: Pinyin — the system for writing Mandarin sounds with Roman letters.
flashcards.example: 我们用拼音学发音。Wǒmen yòng pīnyīn xué fāyīn. (We use pinyin to learn pronunciation.)

flashcards.definition: Tone — the pitch pattern of a syllable; changing it changes the word.
flashcards.example: 汉语有四个声调。Hànyǔ yǒu sì ge shēngdiào. (Chinese has four tones.)

flashcards.definition: Mum, mother. The first syllable is first tone; the second is neutral.
flashcards.example: 我爱妈妈。Wǒ ài māma. (I love my mum.)
那是一匹马。Nà shì yì pǐ mǎ. (That is a horse.)

flashcards.definition: Question particle — neutral tone; added to a statement to make a yes/no question.
flashcards.example: 你好吗？Nǐ hǎo ma? (How are you?)

flashcards.definition: Initial — the consonant at the start of a Mandarin syllable.
flashcards.example: b 是一个声母。b shì yí ge shēngmǔ. (b is an initial.)

flashcards.definition: Final — the vowel part of a Mandarin syllable that follows the initial.
flashcards.example: hǎo 的韵母是 ao。hǎo de yùnmǔ shì ao. (The final of hǎo is ao.)

flashcards.definition: Radical — a character component that hints at meaning, used to organise dictionaries.
flashcards.example: 河 的部首是氵。hé de bùshǒu shì shuǐ (氵). (The radical of 河 is the water radical.)

flashcards.definition: Stroke — one of the basic lines used to write a Chinese character.
flashcards.example: 一 只有一画。yī zhǐyǒu yí huà. (一 has only one stroke.)

flashcards.definition: Person — a simple character that cannot be split into smaller parts.
flashcards.example: 他是中国人。Tā shì Zhōngguó rén. (He is Chinese.)

flashcards.definition: Bright — a compound character made of 日 (sun) and 月 (moon).
River — the 氵(water) radical tells you it relates to water.
flashcards.example: 这条河很长。Zhè tiáo hé hěn cháng. (This river is very long.)

A type of Chinese calligraphy brush
The name of the Chinese alphabet song
questions.explanation: Pinyin (拼音) is the official romanisation system: it spells out how each Chinese character is pronounced using familiar letters, helping learners read, type and look up words.

questions.stem: The character 妈 is written mā in pinyin. Which tone is it?
questions.explanation: The mark ā is the first tone — a high, flat pitch held level, like singing a single note.

questions.stem: How many main tones does Mandarin have (not counting the neutral tone)?
questions.explanation: Mandarin has four main tones (high-level, rising, falling-rising, falling) plus a light neutral tone, giving five pitch patterns in total.

questions.stem: In the word liù (六, six), where does the tone mark go and why?
choices: On the i, because i is always marked
On the u, because in the pair iu the second vowel carries the mark
On both vowels, one mark each
On the l, because it is the initial
questions.explanation: When i and u combine (iu or ui), the tone mark is placed on the second vowel, so liù carries its mark on the u. Tone marks never sit on consonants.
马 mǎ (third tone) means horse. The same letters with other tones give different words: mā mum, mà to scold, ma question particle.

questions.stem: Which tone mark shows the second (rising) tone?
questions.explanation: The acute accent á rises from left to right, matching the rising pitch of the second tone — like the voice going up at the end of a question in English.

questions.stem: A character containing the radical 氵 most likely relates to:
questions.explanation: 氵 is the water radical. Characters such as 河 (river) and 海 (sea) contain it, signalling a connection to water or liquids.

questions.stem: In the syllable hǎo (好), what is the initial?
questions.explanation: The initial is the starting consonant, h. The final is ao, and the third-tone mark sits on the a because a takes priority over o.

questions.stem: A learner says 'wǒ xiǎng mài shuǐguǒ' but means 'I want to buy fruit'. What went wrong?
choices: They used the fourth-tone mài (to sell) instead of the third-tone mǎi (to buy)
They should have said 喝 instead of 买
Fruit cannot be bought, only sold
questions.explanation: 买 mǎi (third tone) means to buy and 卖 mài (fourth tone) means to sell — opposites that differ only in tone. The wrong tone reversed the meaning of the sentence.

questions.stem: When writing the character 十 (ten), which stroke is written first?
choices: The vertical stroke, top to bottom
The horizontal stroke, left to right
Either stroke — order does not matter
Both strokes at the same time
questions.explanation: The rule 'horizontal before vertical' applies: the horizontal line of 十 is drawn first, then the vertical line crosses it. Consistent stroke order keeps characters balanced.

questions.stem: How is the second syllable of 妈妈 (māma) pronounced?
choices: Neutral tone — light and short, with no tone mark
Third tone, dipping down and up
questions.explanation: In repeated-word family terms like 妈妈 and 哥哥, the second syllable takes the neutral tone: short, light and unmarked in pinyin.

questions.stem: The character 明 (míng) is made of 日 (sun) and 月 (moon). What does it mean?
questions.explanation: 明 combines the two brightest objects in the sky — the sun and the moon — to express the idea of brightness. It is a classic example of a compound character.

questions.stem: 好 (hǎo, good) is a compound of 女 (woman) and which other part?
questions.explanation: 好 = 女 + 子. This compound structure — two meaningful parts combined — is how the majority of Chinese characters are built.

questions.stem: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo, with two third tones. How is it actually pronounced in natural speech?
choices: ní hǎo — the first third tone changes to a second tone
nì hào — both become fourth tones
ni hao — both become neutral tones
questions.explanation: Third-tone sandhi: when two third tones meet, the first is pronounced as a second tone to make speech flow. The spelling stays nǐ hǎo, but you say ní hǎo.

questions.stem: Which character most likely relates to speaking?
questions.explanation: 说 shuō (to speak) contains 讠, the speech radical — its meaning clue. 河 has the water radical, 林 the wood radical, and 明 contains the sun.
